title: The boon beyond compare
hookLine: the last gift, Satyavan's life given back, and why women still wind thread round a banyan
carry: a vrat offers your fast for another's long life

cards: Ask once more, says Death. Savitri is still on the road behind Yama, still talking. And this time she asks for something for herself.
Let me have sons, she says, sons of my own, born of Satyavan. Yama grants it. So be it.
She keeps walking, and keeps speaking about the good. A gift has now been given that can only come true one way. And the noose in Yama's hand is still closed.

teach.h: A CONVERSATION WON, NOT A TRAP.
teach.b: In the epic this isn't a clever trap. It's a conversation won.
Savitri speaks again about the good, how they keep to the truth and hold up the world, and Yama, pleased once more, tells her to ask for something beyond compare. Savitri asks plainly.
The gift you gave me can't come true without my husband. Without him I don't want happiness, or heaven, or my own life.
Let Satyavan live. And Yama loosens the noose. Satyavan opens his eyes in her lap like a man waking from a long sleep.
It's night, he's weak and frightened for his parents, so Savitri ties up her hair, helps him up, carries his axe, and they walk home through the dark.

The sage Markandeya, who tells this story to the exiled Pandavas, promises them that Draupadi will save them the same way. Now the teaching. Every year, in the month of Jyeshtha, many married Hindu women keep Vat Savitri.
They fast, worship a banyan tree, wind thread around it, and tell this story aloud.
In popular tellings Satyavan lay under a banyan, a tree that lives for centuries, so it stands for the long life Savitri won.

teach.h: A VRAT FOR ANOTHER'S LONG LIFE.
teach.b: A vrat like this is one of Hinduism's oldest ways to love someone: you give something up yourself, often food, and offer it for another person's long life.
Savitri began with a three-night fast before her husband's last day, and finished with her words on the road.

how: Markandeya ends the story by turning back to Yudhishthira's question about Draupadi. Outside the epic, many married women keep Vat Savitri in Jyeshtha: a fast, worship of a banyan, thread wound round it, and the story told aloud.

o: a boon, a gift granted by a god
a curse spoken by a sage in anger
a promise a bride makes at her wedding

games.q: the end of the road — tap the pairs.
p: sons for Savitri, born of Satyavan
wakes as if from a long sleep
a fast and thread round a banyan

s: in the epic, Savitri simply tricks Death with a loophole
she keeps speaking about the good, and Yama, pleased, asks her to name a gift beyond compare.
Satyavan woke up thinking he had been asleep
he asks why she didn't wake him, and where the dark figure went.
the banyan is used on Vat Savitri because it fruits all year
it lives for centuries, so it stands for long life; in popular tellings Satyavan lay beneath one.

games.q: Sam asks why an aunty fasts all day on Vat Savitri and ties thread round a banyan. what's the best answer?
o: she's keeping a vrat: giving up food and offering it for her husband's long life, as Savitri did.
she's asking the tree to grant her wishes.
games.why: a vrat gives something up and offers it for someone else. Savitri fasted three nights, then talked with Death; the banyan stands for the long life she won.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose long life you wish for, someone you can still call or sit beside, and let their face come clear. Breathe in and notice that they're here; breathe out and wish them years.
If you pray, offer a short prayer for their long life, the way women do on Vat Savitri; if not, simply hold the wish. If someone you've lost comes to mind instead, hold them kindly too.

wordCard.voice: Vara, a boon, the gift Yama kept offering Savitri on the road. A wife who talked with Death until he gave her husband back, and a vow women still keep under the banyan. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit vara: a boon, a gift granted; what Yama keeps offering Savitri on the road.

carryVoice: Your line: a vrat offers your fast for another's long life. She carried the axe, and he leaned on her. Eight hundred days now.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Pativrata-mahatmya Parva (Markandeya's story of Savitri): the fourth boon; Savitri's last speech; Satyavan restored; the walk home; Dyumatsena's sight; Markandeya's conclusion about Draupadi
Vat Savitri vrat (Jyeshtha amavasya; Vat Purnima in Maharashtra and Gujarat): fasting, banyan worship, thread, the Savitri katha; the banyan as Satyavan's resting place in popular tellings
